newsitem.title: USA: Sluggish U.S factories signal slow Q1, tame prices.
newsitem.headline: Sluggish U.S factories signal slow Q1, tame prices.

text.p: U.S. manufacturing output stood still in January, suggesting economic growth is being reined in to a more sustainable level, which explains why inflation is remaining in check, economists said.
The Federal Reserve reported industrial production was unchanged in January, while December's rise in factory output was revised down to 0.5 percent from 0.7 percent.
"Clearly, the economy is running out of steam a little bit from the very robust pace in the final quarter of 1996," said Sung Won Sohn, chief economist at Norwest Coroporation.
"That is one of the reasons why inflation is not receiving any upward pressure," Sohn added.

Released in tandem with the output data was the capacity utilization rate, which fell to 83.3 percent in January from 83.5 percent in December. This suggests production bottlenecks are not threatening to reduce the supply of manufactured goods to the market, which could push up prices, economists said.
The data came right on the heels of an even more remarkable sign of tame inflation in the form of a 0.3-percent drop in the January producer price index on Friday.
The wholesale price drop stood in contrast to an expected 0.3 percent jump and was the first decline since October 1994.
Even more important to economists, the core rate of producer inflation which excludes food and energy prices was steady in January, dashing forecasts of a 0.2 percent rise.

Mike Niemira, an economist at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi Ltd, said the capacity use rate typically moves up and down with the production data, and would not give Federal Reserve policymakers any new information for make credit decisions.
"But it's obviously more good news on top of the PPI report," he added.
Many sectors and product groups experienced a decline in output in January.
Construction supplies declined 0.7 percent as did the production of primary metals. Non-durable goods fell 0.4 percent, led by a 1.4 percent decrease in petroleum products.
One bright spot was a 2.4 percent increase in automobile and light truck production.

"We saw a wide variety of industries and product groups with declining output this month, offsetting a good gain in motor vehicle production," said Carol Stone, senior economist at Nomura Securities International Inc.
Moreover, economists seemed encouraged that the pile of information about the economy released on Friday continued to paint one of the best possible pictures for U.S. credit markets.
"This whole collection of data continues to (support) moderate growth and low inflation that doesn't need ... preventive work from the Federal Reserve," Stone said.
